data.scenario_text: The function L(x)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)\right]+30 models the water level, in feet, of a reservoir, where x=1 represents January, x=2 represents February, and so on.
data.part_a: What is the average water level of the reservoir?
data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in November. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=30, so the reservoir averages \boxed{30\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=30+8=38\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=30-8=22\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in July at 38\text{ ft} and lowest in January at 22\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[22\text{ ft},\ 38\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and is lowest in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-4)\right]+30=8\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+30

=8\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+30=26

So the model gives exactly \boxed{26.0\text{ ft}} in November.

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)\right]+14 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 7:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

d(7)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+14

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=33, so the rider averages \boxed{33\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=33+20=53\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=33-20=13\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 53\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 13\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[13\text{ ft},\ 53\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (9:00 a.m.):

d(9)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+12

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

\text{maximum}=31+20=51\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=31-20=11\text{ ft}

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the household's electricity use in May. Round to the nearest kilowatt-hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=828, so the household averages \boxed{828\text{ kWh}} per month.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=122, so the quantity rises 122 above the average value and falls 122 below it:

\text{maximum}=828+122=950\text{ kWh}\qquad\text{minimum}=828-122=706\text{ kWh}

The heaviest use is in July at 950\text{ kWh} and the lightest is in January at 706\text{ kWh}, so the range of monthly use is \boxed{[706\text{ kWh},\ 950\text{ kWh}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so use follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: use is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and bottoms out in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

E(5)=122\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-4)\right]+828=122\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+828

=122\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+828=889

data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=40, so the rider averages \boxed{40\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=22, so the quantity rises 22 above the average value and falls 22 below it:

\text{maximum}=40+22=62\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=40-22=18\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 62\text{ ft} at 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 18\text{ ft} at 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[18\text{ ft},\ 62\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=7 (at 7 minutes after the ride starts):

H(7)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-2)\right]+40=22\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+40

=22\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+40=51

So the model gives exactly \boxed{51.0\text{ ft}} at 7 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)+14

=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

So the model gives approximately \boxed{10.5\text{ ft}} at noon.

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=38, so the rider averages \boxed{38\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=38+16=54\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=38-16=22\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 54\text{ ft} at 6 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 22\text{ ft} at 12 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[22\text{ ft},\ 54\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)=0 \implies t-3=0 \implies t=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 3 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 3 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 6 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 12 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=5 (at 5 minutes after the ride starts):

H(5)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+38=16\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+38

=16\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+38=\frac{16\sqrt{3}}{2}+38

So the model gives approximately \boxed{51.9\text{ ft}} at 5 minutes after the ride starts.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid f(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=51, so the average temperature is \boxed{51^\circ\text{F}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=51+20=71^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=51-20=31^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[31^\circ\text{F},\ 71^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in May, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is August and the coolest is February.

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (September):

f(9)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+51=20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+51

=20\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+51=\frac{20\sqrt{3}}{2}+51

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=55+20=75^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=55-20=35^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[35^\circ\text{F},\ 75^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in May, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is August and the coolest is February.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

f(7)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+55=20\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+55

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in December. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=18, so the reservoir averages \boxed{18\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=18+8=26\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=18-8=10\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in July at 26\text{ ft} and lowest in January at 10\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 26\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} months, and so the pattern is shifted 4 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in April, peaks in July, and is lowest in January.

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (December):

L(12)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-4)\right]+18=8\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+18

=8\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+18=-\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{2}+18

So the model gives approximately \boxed{11.1\text{ ft}} in December.

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)\right]+14 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 5:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 20\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 20\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (5:00 a.m.):

d(5)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-4)\right]+14=6\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+14

=6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+14=17

So the model gives exactly \boxed{17.0\text{ ft}} at 5:00 a.m..

data.scenario_text: The function H(t)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right]+32 models a rider's height, in feet, above the ground on a Ferris wheel, where t is the number of minutes after the ride starts.
data.part_a: What is the rider's average height above the ground during one full revolution?
data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height at 9 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=32, so the rider averages \boxed{32\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=22, so the quantity rises 22 above the average value and falls 22 below it:

\text{maximum}=32+22=54\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=32-22=10\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 54\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 10\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 54\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

The phase shift is \boxed{1} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 1 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 1 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 4 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 10 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=9 (at 9 minutes after the ride starts):

H(9)=22\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-1)\right]+32=22\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+32

=22\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+32=-\frac{22\sqrt{3}}{2}+32

So the model gives approximately \boxed{12.9\text{ ft}} at 9 minutes after the ride starts.

data.scenario_text: The function V(x)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)\right]+31 models the number of visitors, in thousands, to a national park in month x of the year, where x=1 represents January.
data.part_a: What is the average number of visitors the park receives per month, in thousands?
data.part_b: What is the range of the park's monthly number of visitors, in thousands?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of visitors in July. Round to the nearest thousand visitors.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=31, so the park averages \boxed{31\text{ thousand}} visitors per month.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=20, so the quantity rises 20 above the average value and falls 20 below it:

\text{maximum}=31+20=51\text{ thousand}\qquad\text{minimum}=31-20=11\text{ thousand}

The busiest month is May with 51\text{ thousand} visitors and the slowest is November with 11\text{ thousand}, so the range is \boxed{[11\text{ thousand},\ 51\text{ thousand}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so visitation follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} months, and so the pattern is shifted 2 months to the right: attendance is at its average and climbing in February, peaks in May, and is lowest in November.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

V(7)=20\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-2)\right]+31=20\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+31

=20\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+31=41

So the model gives exactly \boxed{41\text{ thousand}} visitors in July.
